function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a practical, step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run manually) to accomplish everything you asked for.  
I’ll walk through the commands, explain what each one does, and show the exact files that will be created/updated.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git push`, or any other network‑dependent commands from here, but the script below will work on any machine that has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `yq` (or `jq`) installed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1 Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

```bash
# 2.1.1 List the files
tree -L 2
```

Typical output (you may see something like this):

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── src
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

* `src/index.js` – the main entry point of the Node.js app.  
* `package.json` – contains dependencies and start script (`"start": "node src/index.js"`).  
* No existing Dockerfile or Kubernetes manifests.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a minimal Dockerfile that uses the official Node.js slim image, copies the source, installs deps, and runs the app.

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY src ./src

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["npm", "start"]
EOF
```

> Adjust the Node version (`node:18-alpine`) if you prefer a different base image.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a `k8s` directory and add a deployment + service manifest.

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
cat > k8s/deployment.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
EOF
```

> Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name/tag you’ll push to later.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Add a `.github/workflows/build.yml` that builds the Docker image, pushes it to GitHub Container Registry, and optionally deploys to a cluster.

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/build.yml <<'EOF'
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: k8s/*.yaml
        images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
EOF
```

> *If you don’t have a `KUBECONFIG` secret, skip the “Deploy” step or remove that job entirely.*

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`. It will build the image, push it to GHCR, and (if configured) deploy to your cluster.

---

## Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile exists
cat Dockerfile

# Verify Kubernetes YAML
cat k8s/deployment.yaml

# Verify GitHub Actions workflow
cat .github/workflows/build.yml
```

Run `docker build -t test-image .` locally to ensure the Dockerfile works before pushing.

---

### Recap of what was added

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/build.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

That’s it! Once you push, the workflow will take care of building and publishing the image, and you’ll have a ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes configuration. Happy coding!
